claim: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is a neurovascular disease characterized by accumulation of the amyloid-β peptide in the brain vasculature, which ultimately leads to stroke and cognitive decline.
source: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is a neurovascular disease characterized by accumulation of the amyloid-β peptide in the brain vasculature, which ultimately leads to stroke and cognitive decline (Banerjee et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Banerjee et al., 2017, which provides external scholarly support for this definition and characterization of CAA.

claim: In both hereditary and sporadic variants of CAA, impairments in cerebrovascular function can be found early in the disease process.
source: In both hereditary and sporadic variants of CAA, measurements in patients have shown that impairments in cerebrovascular function can be found early in the disease process (Dumas et al., 2012; van Opstal et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dumas et al., 2012 and van Opstal et al., 2017, which provide evidence from patient measurements.

claim: Cerebrovascular function impairments in CAA patients were measured with blood oxygenation level dependent-functional magnetic resonance imaging (BOLD-fMRI) and a visual stimulation paradigm.
source: These measurements were performed with blood oxygenation level dependent-functional magnetic resonance imaging (BOLD-fMRI) and a visual stimulation paradigm, allowing to characterize the cerebrovascular response to neuronal activation in the occipital cortex, where visual processing occurs.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the referenced patient studies, drawing from the cited literature.

claim: The occipital cortex is where CAA burden is highest.
source: The occipital cortex is also where CAA burden is highest (Yamada et al., 1987), likely contributing to the sensitivity of the fMRI measurement.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yamada et al., 1987.

claim: The transgenic Swedish Dutch Iowa (Tg-SwDI) mouse model expresses low levels of the human amyloid-β precursor protein (APP) gene with three familial mutations.
source: The transgenic Swedish Dutch Iowa (Tg-SwDI) mouse model is an amyloidosis model expressing low levels of the human amyloid-β precursor protein (APP) gene with three familial mutations, of which the Dutch and Iowa mutations are located in the amyloid-β coding region of APP (Davis et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davis et al., 2004, which describes the genetic characteristics of the Tg-SwDI model.

claim: The Dutch and Iowa mutations in the Tg-SwDI model are located in the amyloid-β coding region of APP.
source: The transgenic Swedish Dutch Iowa (Tg-SwDI) mouse model is an amyloidosis model expressing low levels of the human amyloid-β precursor protein (APP) gene with three familial mutations, of which the Dutch and Iowa mutations are located in the amyloid-β coding region of APP (Davis et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davis et al., 2004.

claim: Amyloid-β accumulation in the Tg-SwDI model starts around 6 months of age.
source: The neuronal expression of the mutated APP in this model leads to early amyloid-β accumulation in the brain, starting around 6 months.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the Tg-SwDI model, likely derived from the literature.

claim: Amyloid-β accumulates predominantly around capillaries in the Tg-SwDI model.
source: Amyloid-β accumulates predominantly around capillaries in the Tg-SwDI model, which is similar to a subtype of CAA pathology observed in pathological examinations of patient tissue and sometimes referred to as capCAA (Thal et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thal et al., 2002, which describes capCAA pathology.

claim: Capillary amyloid-β accumulation in the Tg-SwDI model is similar to a subtype of CAA pathology observed in patient tissue, referred to as capCAA.
source: Amyloid-β accumulates predominantly around capillaries in the Tg-SwDI model, which is similar to a subtype of CAA pathology observed in pathological examinations of patient tissue and sometimes referred to as capCAA (Thal et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thal et al., 2002.

claim: Vascular pathology in the Tg-SwDI model is most severe in the thalamus.
source: Unlike patients, vascular pathology in the Tg-SwDI model is most severe in the thalamus (Miao et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miao et al., 2005.

claim: Previous studies reported early impairments in cerebrovascular reactivity (CVR) in Tg-SwDI mice using laser Doppler flowmetry (LDF) after skull removal.
source: Previous studies have measured cortical vascular reactivity using laser Doppler flowmetry (LDF) after removal of the skull in Tg-SwDI and wild-type (WT) mice. They reported, similar to CAA patients, early impairments in cerebrovascular reactivity (CVR) in Tg-SwDI mice (Chow et al., 2007; Park et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chow et al., 2007 and Park et al., 2014.

claim: Arterial spin labeling (ASL)-MRI uses magnetically labeled arterial blood as an endogenous tracer to measure tissue perfusion.
source: With ASL, arterial blood is magnetically labeled and used as endogenous tracer flowing into the tissue of interest, which is most often the brain. The distribution of the label over the different brain regions reflects local tissue perfusion and can be converted into absolute cerebral blood flow (CBF) values, expressed as mL/100 g/min.
evidence: This claim describes the established methodology of ASL-MRI, representing general scientific knowledge about the technique.

claim: ASL-MRI can be combined with a hypercapnic challenge to determine both CBF and CVR for different brain regions.
source: When combined with a hypercapnic challenge, both CBF and CVR can be determined for different brain regions.
evidence: This claim describes a standard application of ASL-MRI methodology.

claim: ASL may underestimate CBF in cases of slow flow due to delayed arterial transit time (ATT).
source: A known unfavorable characteristic of ASL is a possible underestimation of CBF in case of slow flow. In that case, a delayed arterial transit time (ATT) – the time that it takes for the label to travel from the labeling plane to the brain tissue – could be misinterpreted as decreased CBF.
evidence: This claim describes a known limitation of ASL methodology, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: ATT evaluation is valuable to prevent potential underestimation of ASL-based CBF estimates.
source: ATT evaluation is therefore valuable to prevent a potential underestimation of the ASL-based CBF estimates, as well as indicative in itself of vascular pathology (Alsop et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alsop et al., 2015.

claim: ATT is indicative of vascular pathology.
source: ATT evaluation is therefore valuable to prevent a potential underestimation of the ASL-based CBF estimates, as well as indicative in itself of vascular pathology (Alsop et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alsop et al., 2015.

claim: Hypercapnia consistently induced a CBF increase in both WT and Tg-SwDI mice under isoflurane anesthesia.
source: Hypercapnia consistently induced a CBF increase in both WT and Tg-SwDI mice under isoflurane anesthesia (Figure 2 and Figure 3), which was mainly located in cortical regions (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 2 and 3, showing CBF responses to hypercapnia.

claim: The CBF increase induced by hypercapnia was mainly located in cortical regions.
source: Hypercapnia consistently induced a CBF increase in both WT and Tg-SwDI mice under isoflurane anesthesia (Figure 2 and Figure 3), which was mainly located in cortical regions (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2, which displays CBF maps showing regional distribution of the response.

claim: No significant differences were observed in baseline CBF between Tg-SwDI and WT mice at any time point.
source: Surprisingly, the CBF maps and CBF time profiles acquired in the mid-brain of the Tg-SwDI mice resembled those of the WT mice at every time point. Hence no significant differences were observed in baseline CBF nor CVR between the two genotypes at any time point (Figure 3b; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for individual animal trends).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant differences were observed in CVR between Tg-SwDI and WT mice at any time point.
source: Surprisingly, the CBF maps and CBF time profiles acquired in the mid-brain of the Tg-SwDI mice resembled those of the WT mice at every time point. Hence no significant differences were observed in baseline CBF nor CVR between the two genotypes at any time point (Figure 3b; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for individual animal trends).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Age had a significant effect on CBF in both WT and Tg-SwDI mice.
source: A significant effect of age on CBF was, however, observed in both WT and Tg-SwDI mice, χ2(3)=13.00, p=0.005 and χ2(3)=8.49, p=0.037, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (Friedman test) of the longitudinal data.

claim: Baseline CBF significantly decreased between 3 and 6 months of age in WT mice.
source: Post hoc analysis indicated that this was attributable to a decrease in baseline CBF between the ages of 3 and 6 months. Between these time points, median (iqr) CBF significantly decreased from 155 (143–159) to 121 (112–124) mL/100 g/min in WT mice, p=0.008.
evidence: This claim is supported by post hoc statistical analysis of the longitudinal CBF data.

claim: Baseline CBF decreased from 147 (133–151) to 126 (103–135) mL/100 g/min between 3 and 6 months in Tg-SwDI mice, but this was not statistically significant after Bonferroni correction.
source: In Tg-SwDI mice, a similar trend was observed, from 147 (133–151) to 126 (103–135) mL/100 g/min, p=0.036, but this was not significant (cut-off p-value of 0.017 after Bonferroni correction).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the longitudinal CBF data in Tg-SwDI mice.

claim: From 6 months of age, baseline CBF remained stable in both WT and Tg-SwDI groups.
source: From 6 months of age, the baseline CBF remained stable inside each group.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the longitudinal CBF data.

claim: Age had a significant effect on CVR in WT mice.
source: Age also had a significant effect on CVR in WT mice, χ2(3)=8.33, p=0.040.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (Friedman test) of the longitudinal CVR data.

claim: There was a trend toward increased CVR between 3 and 6 months in WT mice, from 13 (7–17) to 31 (23–37) %, but this did not reach significance in post hoc analysis.
source: No differences were observed with post hoc analysis, however, besides a trend toward increased CVR between the ages of 3 and 6 months, from 13 (7–17) to 31 (23–37) %, p=0.038.
evidence: This claim is supported by post hoc statistical analysis of the CVR data.

claim: Age had no significant effect on CVR in Tg-SwDI mice.
source: Age had no significant effect on CVR in Tg-SwDI mice, χ2(3)=6.94, p=0.074.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (Friedman test) of the longitudinal CVR data.

claim: No differences were observed in cortical and thalamic CBF and CVR between WT and Tg-SwDI mice.
source: Additional analysis in cortical and thalamic areas did not reveal any difference between WT and Tg-SwDI mice either (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: No differences were observed in brain volume between WT and Tg-SwDI mice.
source: Similarly, no differences were observed in brain volume, body weight, change in tc-pCO2 upon the hypercapnia challenges, respiration rate, and inversion efficiency between WT and Tg-SwDI mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the supplementary figures.

claim: No differences were observed in body weight between WT and Tg-SwDI mice.
source: Similarly, no differences were observed in brain volume, body weight, change in tc-pCO2 upon the hypercapnia challenges, respiration rate, and inversion efficiency between WT and Tg-SwDI mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the supplementary figures.

claim: No differences were observed in change in tc-pCO2 upon hypercapnia challenges between WT and Tg-SwDI mice.
source: Similarly, no differences were observed in brain volume, body weight, change in tc-pCO2 upon the hypercapnia challenges, respiration rate, and inversion efficiency between WT and Tg-SwDI mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the supplementary figures.

claim: No differences were observed in respiration rate between WT and Tg-SwDI mice.
source: Similarly, no differences were observed in brain volume, body weight, change in tc-pCO2 upon the hypercapnia challenges, respiration rate, and inversion efficiency between WT and Tg-SwDI mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the supplementary figures.

claim: No differences were observed in inversion efficiency between WT and Tg-SwDI mice.
source: Similarly, no differences were observed in brain volume, body weight, change in tc-pCO2 upon the hypercapnia challenges, respiration rate, and inversion efficiency between WT and Tg-SwDI mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the supplementary figures.

claim: Median baseline ATT values in the mid-brain at 12 months were 206 (186-240) ms for WT mice and 223 (202–246) ms for Tg-SwDI mice.
source: Median (iqr) baseline ATT values in the mid-brain were also similar for both WT and Tg-SwDI mice, i.e. 206 (186-240) milliseconds (ms) and 223 (202–246) ms respectively at 12 months of age (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATT measurements presented in Figure 4.

claim: Hypercapnia shortened the ATT to 192 (189–205) ms for WT mice and 197 (187–207) ms for Tg-SwDI mice.
source: The hypercapnia challenge shortened the ATT to 192 (189–205) for WT and 197 (187–207) for Tg-SwDI mice, which was significant for Tg-SwDI mice (Z = −2.20 and p=0.028), but did not reach significance for WT mice (Z = −1.84 and p=0.066).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATT measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: The ATT shortening with hypercapnia was significant for Tg-SwDI mice (Z = −2.20 and p=0.028).
source: The hypercapnia challenge shortened the ATT to 192 (189–205) for WT and 197 (187–207) for Tg-SwDI mice, which was significant for Tg-SwDI mice (Z = −2.20 and p=0.028), but did not reach significance for WT mice (Z = −1.84 and p=0.066).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ATT data.

claim: The ATT shortening with hypercapnia did not reach significance for WT mice (Z = −1.84 and p=0.066).
source: The hypercapnia challenge shortened the ATT to 192 (189–205) for WT and 197 (187–207) for Tg-SwDI mice, which was significant for Tg-SwDI mice (Z = −2.20 and p=0.028), but did not reach significance for WT mice (Z = −1.84 and p=0.066).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ATT data.

claim: Changing from isoflurane to urethane and alpha-chloralose (U and A) anesthesia resulted in profound hemodynamic changes.
source: The change of anesthesia protocol resulted in profound hemodynamic changes: baseline CBF was markedly reduced and the hypercapnic response was higher in amplitude, but also slower (Figure 5a), and more widespread in the brain tissue (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5a and 5b comparing the two anesthesia protocols.

claim: Under U and A anesthesia, baseline CBF was markedly reduced compared to isoflurane anesthesia.
source: The change of anesthesia protocol resulted in profound hemodynamic changes: baseline CBF was markedly reduced and the hypercapnic response was higher in amplitude, but also slower (Figure 5a), and more widespread in the brain tissue (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Under U and A anesthesia, the hypercapnic response was higher in amplitude but slower compared to isoflurane anesthesia.
source: The change of anesthesia protocol resulted in profound hemodynamic changes: baseline CBF was markedly reduced and the hypercapnic response was higher in amplitude, but also slower (Figure 5a), and more widespread in the brain tissue (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5a.

claim: Under U and A anesthesia, the hypercapnic response was more widespread in the brain tissue compared to isoflurane anesthesia.
source: The change of anesthesia protocol resulted in profound hemodynamic changes: baseline CBF was markedly reduced and the hypercapnic response was higher in amplitude, but also slower (Figure 5a), and more widespread in the brain tissue (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5b.

claim: Median CBF decreased from 126 (84–141) to 28 (26–30) mL/100 g/min in WT mice when switching from isoflurane to U and A anesthesia (Z = −2.67 and p=0.008).
source: The CBF and CVR estimates were indeed significantly impacted by the change in anesthesia protocol (Figure 5c), with the median CBF (iqr) decreasing from 126 (84–141) to 28 (26–30) mL/100 g/min in WT mice, Z = −2.67 and p=0.008, and median (iqr) CVR increasing from 26 (6–47) to 233 (193–245) %, Z = −2.67 and p=0.008.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of CBF data comparing the two anesthesia protocols.

claim: Median CVR increased from 26 (6–47) to 233 (193–245) % in WT mice when switching from isoflurane to U and A anesthesia (Z = −2.67 and p=0.008).
source: The CBF and CVR estimates were indeed significantly impacted by the change in anesthesia protocol (Figure 5c), with the median CBF (iqr) decreasing from 126 (84–141) to 28 (26–30) mL/100 g/min in WT mice, Z = −2.67 and p=0.008, and median (iqr) CVR increasing from 26 (6–47) to 233 (193–245) %, Z = −2.67 and p=0.008.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of CVR data comparing the two anesthesia protocols.

claim: Median CBF decreased from 114 (103–130) to 25 (21–40) mL/100 g/min in Tg-SwDI mice when switching from isoflurane to U and A anesthesia (Z = −2.37 and p=0.018).
source: These changes were again comparable to those in Tg-SwDI mice, with the median CBF (iqr) and CVR (iqr) respectively changing from 114 (103–130) to 25 (21–40) mL/100 g/min, Z = −2.37 and p=0.018, and from 30 (17–34) to 265 (178–312) %, Z = −2.37 and p=0.018.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of CBF data comparing the two anesthesia protocols.

claim: Median CVR increased from 30 (17–34) to 265 (178–312) % in Tg-SwDI mice when switching from isoflurane to U and A anesthesia (Z = −2.37 and p=0.018).
source: These changes were again comparable to those in Tg-SwDI mice, with the median CBF (iqr) and CVR (iqr) respectively changing from 114 (103–130) to 25 (21–40) mL/100 g/min, Z = −2.37 and p=0.018, and from 30 (17–34) to 265 (178–312) %, Z = −2.37 and p=0.018.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of CVR data comparing the two anesthesia protocols.

claim: The CBF response at the induction phase of U and A anesthesia was similar in Tg-SwDI and WT mice.
source: The CBF response at the induction phase of U and A anesthesia was also similar in Tg-SwDI and WT mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The tc-pCO2 responses to hypercapnia challenges increased from an average of 15 mmHg during isoflurane to an average of 19 mmHg during U and A.
source: The higher CVR during U and A was unlikely due to a higher CO2 absorption, as the tc-pCO2 responses to the hypercapnia challenges only increased from an average of 15 mmHG during isoflurane to an average of 19 mmHG during U and A (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by tc-pCO2 measurements presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: No differences in CVR could be observed between WT and Tg-SwDI mice with either MRI or LDF in cohort 2.
source: No differences in CVR could be observed between WT and Tg-SwDI mice, neither with MRI nor with LDF (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6 comparing MRI and LDF measurements.

claim: Removal of the skull severely reduced the CVR for both MRI and LDF imaging modalities.
source: Of note, removal of the skull severely reduced the CVR for both imaging modalities (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: All Tg-SwDI mice developed extensive amyloid-β plaque pathology by the end of the experiment.
source: All Tg-SwDI mice developed extensive amyloid-β plaque pathology by the end of the experiment, with mainly diffuse parenchymal plaques in the cortex and microvascular plaques in the hippocampus and thalamus, but none of the WT mice displayed any amyloid-β deposition (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Tg-SwDI mice showed mainly diffuse parenchymal plaques in the cortex and microvascular plaques in the hippocampus and thalamus.
source: All Tg-SwDI mice developed extensive amyloid-β plaque pathology by the end of the experiment, with mainly diffuse parenchymal plaques in the cortex and microvascular plaques in the hippocampus and thalamus, but none of the WT mice displayed any amyloid-β deposition (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 7.

claim: None of the WT mice displayed any amyloid-β deposition.
source: All Tg-SwDI mice developed extensive amyloid-β plaque pathology by the end of the experiment, with mainly diffuse parenchymal plaques in the cortex and microvascular plaques in the hippocampus and thalamus, but none of the WT mice displayed any amyloid-β deposition (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The findings contradict earlier results obtained in the same Tg-SwDI model.
source: This contradicts previous findings, which showed early impairments in CVR in the cerebral cortex in Tg-SwDI mice using LDF (Chow et al., 2007; Park et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim compares the current study's findings to previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: Differences in anesthesia protocol significantly influence CVR experiments.
source: A likely candidate was the difference in anesthesia protocol, as this has been shown to significantly influence CVR experiments (Petrinovic et al., 2016; Munting et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Petrinovic et al., 2016 and Munting et al., 2019.

claim: ASL-MRI and LDF are sensitive to different blood components (flux of blood plasma vs. velocity of red blood cells).
source: Another likely candidate was the difference in imaging modality, as ASL-MRI and LDF are sensitive to different blood components, namely flux of blood plasma (ASL-MRI) or velocity of red blood cells (LDF).
evidence: This claim describes established technical differences between the two imaging modalities.

claim: Microvascular amyloidosis in the Tg-SwDI mouse model does not induce cerebrovascular dysfunction.
source: However, after differences in anesthesia protocol and imaging modality were accounted for, cerebrovascular function was in our hands still found to be preserved in the Tg-SwDI model.
evidence: This claim is based on the comprehensive experimental data from the study.

claim: The study convincingly shows that microvascular amyloidosis in the Tg-SwDI mouse model does not induce cerebrovascular dysfunction by showing similar findings for two modalities and two anesthesia protocols.
source: However, by showing similar findings for two modalities and two anesthesia protocols, including the ones used before, we think that our study convincingly shows that microvascular amyloidosis in the Tg-SwDI mouse model does not induce cerebrovascular dysfunction.
evidence: This claim is based on the comprehensive experimental design and results of the study.

claim: The robustness of the methods to sense local hemodynamic changes was confirmed by observed reduced CBF and CVR as a function of age and anesthesia.
source: Moreover, the robustness to sense local hemodynamic changes could be confirmed based on the observed reduced CBF and CVR as a function of age and anesthesia.
evidence: This claim is based on the observed effects of age and anesthesia on hemodynamic parameters in the study.

claim: Homozygotic Tg-SwDI mice develop more extensive amyloid-β pathology than hemizygous mice, but with similar distribution and amyloid-β−40/amyloid-β−42 ratios.
source: Homozygotic Tg-SwDI mice have been reported to develop more extensive amyloid-β pathology, but with a similar distribution on the micro- and macro-scale in the brain, and similar amyloid-β−40/amyloid-β−42 ratios as hemizygous mice (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2007.

claim: The amyloid-β pathology found in this study is comparable to what is described in the literature for both hemizygous and homozygous Tg-SwDI mice.
source: Furthermore, the amyloid-β pathology found here (Figure 7) is comparable to what is described in the literature for both hemizygous and homozygous mice, namely diffuse parenchymal plaques in the cortex and microvascular accumulation in the thalamus and hippocampus (Miao et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the study's histological findings (Figure 7) with literature (Miao et al., 2005).

claim: The pCO2 increase measured through the skin during U and A is comparable to that reported with blood gas sampling in Park et al., 2014 (approximately 20 mmHg).
source: Furthermore, the pCO2 increase measured here through the skin during U and A is comparable to that reported with blood gas sampling in Park et al., 2014 (approximately 20 mmHg).
evidence: This claim compares the study's pCO2 measurements to those reported in Park et al., 2014.

claim: Patient studies have shown baseline perfusion deficits in CAA.
source: However, this is not likely to explain the differences in outcomes, as Park et al., 2014 showed impaired responses in Tg-SwDI mice to both hypercapnia and neuronal activity. Furthermore, patient studies have also shown baseline perfusion deficits (van Opstal et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to van Opstal et al., 2017.

claim: Edema was observed with MRI after craniotomy in cohort 2 mice.
source: However, even though the brain surface in these animals was visually normal (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) after the craniotomy, edema was observed with MRI, and with both imaging modalities marked reductions in CBF and CVR were measured in the underlying brain regions in both WT and Tg-SwDI mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by MRI observations presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Marked reductions in CBF and CVR were measured in brain regions underlying the craniotomy in both WT and Tg-SwDI mice.
source: However, even though the brain surface in these animals was visually normal (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) after the craniotomy, edema was observed with MRI, and with both imaging modalities marked reductions in CBF and CVR were measured in the underlying brain regions in both WT and Tg-SwDI mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from both MRI and LDF measurements presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cortical spreading depression (CSD) occurs even at minor manipulations on the dura.
source: A likely explanation for the functional impairments after craniotomy is the occurrence of a cortical spreading depression (CSD), which occurs even at minor manipulations on the dura (Ayata et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ayata et al., 2004.

claim: In mice, CSDs have been reported to cause a CBF reduction of 40–50%.
source: In mice specifically, CSDs have been reported to cause a CBF reduction of 40–50%, and enhanced resistance to relaxation by acetylcholine (Ayata et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ayata et al., 2004.

claim: CSDs in mice cause enhanced resistance to relaxation by acetylcholine.
source: In mice specifically, CSDs have been reported to cause a CBF reduction of 40–50%, and enhanced resistance to relaxation by acetylcholine (Ayata et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ayata et al., 2004.

claim: A recent study reported that skull removal was necessary to detect cerebrovascular dysfunction in a different mouse model of amyloid-β accumulation.
source: Interestingly, a recent study also reported that skull removal was necessary to detect cerebrovascular dysfunction in a different mouse model of amyloid-β accumulation, providing some support for this hypothesis (Sharp et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sharp et al., 2020.

claim: The APP23 model showed early impairments in cerebrovascular function in a noninvasive setup.
source: However, other amyloidosis models did show early impairments in cerebrovascular function, even in a noninvasive set-up, such as the APP23 model (Mueggler et al., 2002; Maier et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mueggler et al., 2002 and Maier et al., 2014.

claim: The APP23 model mainly shows arteriolar CAA pathology.
source: Because the APP23 model mainly shows arteriolar CAA pathology (Sturchler-Pierrat et al., 1997), altogether this might indicate that predominantly CAA pathology on the arteriolar side of the vasculature is responsible for the observed CBF and CVR impairments in patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sturchler-Pierrat et al., 1997.

claim: Hypoxia-induced factor angiopoietin-4 was found to be highly expressed in capCAA patients.
source: Indeed, hypoxia-induced factor angiopoietin-4 was found to be highly expressed in capCAA patients (Chakraborty et al., 2018), indicating that possibly capCAA could induce hypoxic conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chakraborty et al., 2018.

claim: U and A anesthesia is considered one of the more suitable anesthesia protocols for cerebral hemodynamic studies in mice.
source: Interestingly, U and A is considered one of the more suitable anesthesia protocols for cerebral hemodynamic studies in mice, as this protocol has been reported to have relatively mild hemodynamic effects (Janssen et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2010) and to maintain cerebral autoregulation (Dalkara et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Janssen et al., 2004, Wang et al., 2010, and Dalkara et al., 1995.

claim: U and A anesthesia maintains cerebral autoregulation.
source: Interestingly, U and A is considered one of the more suitable anesthesia protocols for cerebral hemodynamic studies in mice, as this protocol has been reported to have relatively mild hemodynamic effects (Janssen et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2010) and to maintain cerebral autoregulation (Dalkara et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dalkara et al., 1995.

claim: The stable hemodynamics during U and A anesthesia come together with very low baseline CBF.
source: However, these studies did not provide absolute CBF estimates, and our results indicate that the stable hemodynamics come together with very low baseline CBF, which may not always be favorable and certainly do not represent normal baseline physiology.
evidence: This claim is based on the study's CBF measurements under U and A anesthesia.

claim: CVR measurements with ASL-MRI were nearly twice as high compared to those obtained with LDF in cohort 2.
source: Both readouts consistently reported preservation of cerebrovascular function in Tg-SwDI mice and a severe reduction of CVR after craniotomy, but CVR measurements with ASL-MRI were nearly twice as high compared to those obtained with LDF.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of CVR measurements from ASL-MRI and LDF in the study.

claim: Hematocrit has been reported to decrease during hypercapnia in the rat brain.
source: Indeed, hematocrit has been reported to decrease during hypercapnia in the rat brain (Keyeux et al., 1995), but with only a 10% decrease during a 10% CO2 challenge, which is too low to explain the observed difference.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Keyeux et al., 1995.

claim: By varying the fiber separation distance in the LDF probe, which changes the measured cortical depth, a different CBF response was measured.
source: The authors showed that by varying the fiber separation distance in the LDF probe, which changes the measured cortical depth, a different CBF response was measured.
evidence: This claim refers to findings from He et al., 2007, describing their experimental observations.

claim: When larger cortical depths were measured with LDF, the technique underestimated the CBF response compared to ASL-MRI.
source: The authors measured CBF responses to electrical whisker stimulation through a thinned skull in rats under urethane anesthesia, and concluded that when larger cortical depths were measured, LDF underestimated the CBF response.
evidence: This claim refers to conclusions from He et al., 2007.

claim: The absolute CBF responses measured with ASL-MRI by He et al., 2007 were comparable to those measured in this study.
source: Interestingly, the absolute CBF responses measured with ASL-MRI by He et al., 2007 were comparable to those measured here.

source: Lastly, another finding in our study that is of interest is the observation of edema and the local reduction in CBF and CVR with MRI after craniotomy. This was observed in all animals, while the brain tissue was normal by visual inspection.
evidence: This claim is based on MRI observations in the study.

claim: Normal appearance of brain tissue is not enough to conclude that the brain tissue is healthy when working with acutely prepared cranial windows.
source: Normal appearance of brain tissue is therefore not enough to conclude that the brain tissue is healthy when working with acutely prepared cranial windows.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the study's observations of edema despite normal visual appearance.

claim: Cerebrovascular function in the Tg-SwDI mouse model of microvascular amyloidosis is preserved up to 12 months of age, despite high amyloid-β burden.
source: In conclusion, this study shows that cerebrovascular function in the Tg-SwDI mouse model of microvascular amyloidosis is preserved up to 12 months of age, despite the high amyloid-β burden observed at that age.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main finding of the study, supported by the comprehensive experimental data.

claim: The observations call into question to what extent microvascular amyloidosis as seen in the Tg-SwDI mouse model is a correct model for cerebrovascular dysfunction as observed in CAA patients.
source: These observations call into question to what extent microvascular amyloidosis as seen in the Tg-SwDI mouse model is a correct model for cerebrovascular dysfunction as observed in CAA patients, and calls for further research to clear up the discrepancy in results.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the study's findings in relation to the existing literature and patient observations.

source: However, to counteract the possibility of a lower effect size, higher standard deviation and/or animal drop-out, we chose to increase our sample size with five animals per group, thus to nine animals per group in total. The cohort consisted of all male mice which were followed longitudinally, that is, they were imaged at 3, 6, 9, 12, and 12.3 months of age.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and sample size of the study.

claim: Two study-related dropouts occurred in the second cohort (one WT and one transgenic) due to failure of the intubation procedure.
